issues.issue: The covenant begins with the bare pronoun "It" and never identifies the covenantor, so the obligor must be supplied from the Section 2.02 chapeau. The prohibition on using "any information relating to the Insurer" is also unbounded — publicly available information appears to be caught.

The broad grant that the Insurer "shall have all rights provided to the Insurer in the Operative Documents" as a third-party beneficiary is cut back by the very next sentence of Section 2.02(j), which confines its third-party beneficiary rights under the Indenture; the interaction of the grant and the limit is not spelled out.

Limiting the Insurer to "the rights granted to it and to the Noteholders in the Indenture" is ambiguous as to whether the Insurer may exercise Noteholder rights or only rights expressly granted to it. The two limbs pull in different directions.

This limitation is in tension with the preceding sentence of Section 2.02(j), which states without qualification that the Insurer has all rights provided to it in the Operative Documents, of which the Indenture is one.

The deeming rule turns notice of a claim based on a mere "alleged violation" of the Truth-in-Lending Act into conclusive notice of an actual breach of a representation, so it is contestable whether an unfounded mortgagor claim triggers the repurchase machinery. "[C]onclusively constitute notice" also does not say whether the breach itself, as opposed to notice of it, is established.

The provision operates on Section 7 of the Depositor Purchase Agreement "as incorporated by reference into the Sale and Servicing Agreement," and its fit with Section 2.01(n), which imports all Operative Document representations directly for the Insurer's benefit, is unclear.

"Any such breach shall be deemed material and the remedies provided in Section 7 of the Depositor Purchase Agreement shall apply, including ..." leaves open whether those remedies are the exclusive consequence or merely additional, and the word "including" before the repurchase and indemnity obligations makes the list non-exhaustive. The indemnity's reach — "all losses, damages, claims and liabilities" — is stated in general terms after specific cost items.

The one-sentence covenant is in the passive voice and names no obligor, and it speaks of "Mortgage Loans" while the rest of the Agreement consistently uses "HELOCs." Whether the two terms are coextensive determines what is covered.
Neither "Mortgage Loans" nor its relation to the defined subject-matter "HELOCs" (used throughout the recitals and Sections 2.01 and 2.02) is settled anywhere in this Agreement.

The prohibition bites on any action or inaction that "may result in a Material Adverse Change," a possibility standard with no threshold, so almost any business decision could be argued to breach it. "[I]nterfere in any material respect with the enforcement of any rights of the Insurer" is similarly unbounded.

Notice is due on "the earlier of" a fixed date and "promptly prior to the date of consummation of such action," which is not a date at all, so the earlier-of formula cannot be applied as written. "[P]romptly prior to" has no fixed content.

The prohibition on mergers and asset transfers is subject to the circular exception "except as provided in the Operative Documents or as permitted hereby," which does not identify any permitted transaction. The exception could swallow the covenant depending on what other documents allow.

"[B]ankruptcy remote entity" is not defined in this Agreement and has no fixed legal content, so the standard the Depositor and Issuer must maintain is unstated. The negative formulation ("shall not cause ... to fail to maintain") further obscures whether it imposes an affirmative duty.

The representation is expressly cut down to a "limited scope of disclosure" defined only by the fact that the Insurer "is not the registrant," so what disclosure the Insurer has actually warranted is left indeterminate. The qualifier is unique in the Agreement and has no measurable boundary.

The confidentiality undertaking is subject to an open-ended string of exceptions — information "requested by appropriate governmental authorities" or disclosure "as necessary to preserve its rights or security under or to enforce the Operative Documents" — whose scope is not fixed. Whether disclosure to reinsurers or rating agencies is an exception or a separate permission is also left to a proviso.

"[C]ommercially reasonable efforts" to obtain an accountants' consent letter is undefined and no benchmark is given for measuring the effort required. The clause also does not say what happens if the letter is not obtained.

"[T]he sole result of such breach shall be" the furnishing obligation operates as an exclusive-remedy clause, but it does not say whether it displaces damages or other remedies otherwise available for a breached representation. Sole-remedy language of this kind is a standard site of dispute.

The trigger refers to "the representation in Section 2.05(i)" no longer being true, but Section 2.05(i) contains a consent, not a representation; the representation is in Section 2.05(j). The mis-citation determines when the Insurer's obligation to furnish financial statements arises.
As written this clause cannot be squared with Section 2.05(j), which says the breach of the Section 2.05(j) representation is what triggers furnishing "pursuant to Section 2.05(k) below."

The trailing qualifier "without regard to affiliations by common control-with the Insurer" is obscure and appears to except from the representation the very category of affiliation most likely to exist. Whether it narrows or negates the no-affiliation statement is genuinely unclear.
